chapter: Chemical Reactions and Equations (Class 10 Science, CBSE)
note: Authored MCQs, 40 per concept, 14 Easy / 13 Medium / 13 Hard.

2727.stem: An equation written with correct formulae but with the atoms not yet equal on both sides is called
2727.explanation: A skeletal equation shows the right substances but has not yet been balanced.

options.why: A balanced equation already has equal atoms on both sides.
A word equation uses names, not formulae at all.
An ionic equation shows ions separately and may still be balanced.

2727.stem: H2 + O2 -> H2O is a skeletal equation because
2727.explanation: There are two oxygen atoms on the left but only one on the right, so the atoms are not yet equal.

options.text: the oxygen atoms are unequal on the two sides

options.why: H2, O2 and H2O are all correct formulae.

options.text: the arrow points the wrong way
options.why: Hydrogen and oxygen are the reactants, so the arrow is correct.

options.text: water cannot be made this way
options.why: Water is genuinely formed when hydrogen burns in oxygen.

2727.stem: The first step in turning a word equation into a balanced one is to write
2727.explanation: The skeletal equation, with correct formulae and no coefficients yet, always comes before balancing.

options.why: Coefficients cannot be chosen until the formulae are on the page.
States are added at the very end, after balancing.
Conditions are added above the arrow once the equation is complete.

2727.stem: In a skeletal equation, the formulae of the substances are
2727.explanation: Formulae must already be correct in a skeletal equation; only the coefficients are still missing.

options.why: An approximate formula would describe a substance that does not exist.
Names belong to a word equation, not a skeletal one.
There would be nothing to balance if the formulae were missing.

2727.stem: Which of these is a skeletal equation?
2727.explanation: Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3 has correct formulae but unequal atoms, which is exactly what skeletal means.

options.why: This one is already balanced, so it is no longer skeletal.
This uses names, so it is a word equation.
This is a statement about a substance, not an equation at all.

2727.stem: Balancing a skeletal equation is done by adding
2727.explanation: Coefficients are placed in front of formulae; subscripts must never be altered.

options.why: Changing a subscript turns the substance into a different compound.
Adding substances changes what the reaction is.
Brackets group atoms within a formula and do not balance anything.

2727.stem: The skeletal equation for the decomposition of water is
2727.explanation: Water breaks into hydrogen and oxygen, both of which are diatomic gases, before any balancing.

options.why: Both gases are diatomic and must be written as molecules.
This is the reverse reaction, the formation of water.
Hydrogen peroxide is a different substance and is not a decomposition product of water.

2727.stem: A skeletal equation is useful mainly because it
2727.explanation: It fixes which substances are involved and in what direction, so balancing can proceed on a settled basis.

options.text: fixes the substances before balancing begins
gives the masses of the reactants
options.why: Masses require balanced coefficients, which are not yet present.

options.text: shows the speed of the reaction
options.why: Rate is never shown by an equation of any kind.
Only experiment can establish that a reaction occurs.

2727.stem: In the skeletal equation Al + Cl2 -> AlCl3, the element that is unbalanced is
2727.explanation: There are two chlorine atoms on the left and three on the right, so chlorine is unbalanced.

options.why: There is one aluminium atom on each side, so it is already balanced.
No oxygen appears anywhere in this equation.
No hydrogen appears anywhere in this equation.

2727.stem: Which statement about a skeletal equation is true?
2727.explanation: A skeletal equation identifies reactants and products correctly but does not yet obey conservation of mass.

options.text: It names the right substances but not the right amounts
It has equal atoms on both sides already
options.why: Equal atoms is what balancing achieves later.
Formulae are exactly what a skeletal equation uses.
Being balanced afterwards is its whole purpose.

2727.stem: The skeletal equation Na + H2O -> NaOH + H2 is unbalanced in
2727.explanation: There are two hydrogen atoms on the left and three on the right, so hydrogen does not balance.

options.why: There is one sodium atom on each side.
There is one oxygen atom on each side.
Counting the hydrogen atoms shows two on the left and three on the right.

2727.stem: Physical states such as (s) and (aq) are usually added to an equation
2727.explanation: States are added after the equation has been balanced, as a final refinement.

options.why: There is nothing to attach a state to before the formulae exist.
States and coefficients carry entirely different information.
Word equations use names and rarely carry state symbols.

2727.stem: Why must formulae be correct before a skeletal equation is balanced?
2727.explanation: Balancing only adjusts how many units react; if a formula is wrong, the balanced result describes the wrong chemistry.

options.text: Balancing cannot repair a wrong formula

options.why: Balancing never touches the formulae, only the coefficients.
Most correct skeletal equations still need coefficients.

options.text: Formulae are optional at this stage
options.why: Without formulae there is no skeletal equation to work with.

2727.stem: The skeletal equation for the reaction of magnesium with hydrochloric acid is
2727.explanation: Magnesium chloride is MgCl2 and hydrogen is diatomic; the equation is skeletal because chlorine and hydrogen are not yet balanced.

options.why: Magnesium has a valency of two and hydrogen gas is diatomic.
This reverses the reaction described.
This omits the acid entirely and describes a different reaction.

2727.stem: Balance Fe + O2 -> Fe2O3. The coefficient needed in front of Fe is
2727.explanation: The balanced form is 4Fe + 3O2 -> 2Fe2O3, so four iron atoms are needed on the left.

options.why: Two iron atoms would balance only one unit of Fe2O3, leaving oxygen unbalanced.
Three is the coefficient needed for oxygen, not for iron.
One iron atom cannot supply the two in a single Fe2O3 unit.

2727.stem: In balancing Al + Cl2 -> AlCl3, the smallest whole-number coefficients are
2727.explanation: Two aluminium atoms and three chlorine molecules give two units of AlCl3, balancing all six chlorine atoms.

options.why: Leaves one chlorine atom unaccounted for on the product side.
Six chlorine atoms on the left cannot fit into one AlCl3 unit.
Reverses the roles of the two coefficients.

2727.stem: Which skeletal equation requires no coefficients at all once written?
2727.explanation: One carbon and one oxygen molecule give exactly one carbon dioxide molecule, so every atom already balances.

options.why: Two oxygen atoms on the left cannot fit into one water molecule.
Neither iron nor oxygen balances as written.
Hydrogen is two on the left and three on the right.

2727.stem: Balancing Na + H2O -> NaOH + H2 gives the coefficient of NaOH as
2727.explanation: The balanced equation is 2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2, so two units of sodium hydroxide are formed.

options.why: One unit leaves sodium and hydrogen both unbalanced.
Three would require three sodium atoms, which the equation does not supply.
Four is twice the smallest whole-number answer.

2727.stem: A student balances an equation and gets coefficients 2, 4, 2, 4. The correct final answer should be
2727.explanation: Convention requires the smallest whole numbers, so every coefficient is halved to give 1, 2, 1, 2.

options.why: Balanced, but not in the smallest whole-number form that convention requires.
Doubles rather than reduces the coefficients.
Dividing each by a different number destroys the balance.

2727.stem: In the skeletal equation CH4 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O, the element to balance last is usually
2727.explanation: Oxygen appears as a free element, and free elements are left to the end because their coefficients can be adjusted without disturbing anything else.

options.why: Carbon appears in only one compound on each side, so it is settled first.
Hydrogen appears in only one compound on each side, so it is settled early.
Order matters a great deal to how quickly the balancing converges.

2727.stem: The skeletal equation KClO3 -> KCl + O2 balances to give the coefficient of O2 as
2727.explanation: The balanced form is 2KClO3 -> 2KCl + 3O2, so three oxygen molecules are released.

options.why: Two oxygen molecules give four atoms, but six are released from two KClO3.
One oxygen molecule cannot carry the three atoms in a single KClO3.
Six molecules would mean twelve atoms, which is twice too many.

2727.stem: Why is Zn + HCl -> ZnCl2 + H2 described as skeletal rather than balanced?
2727.explanation: There is one chlorine and one hydrogen on the left but two of each on the right, so the atoms do not yet match.

options.text: Chlorine and hydrogen are unequal on the two sides

options.why: Zinc appears once on each side, which is already balanced.

options.text: The formula of the acid is wrong
options.why: HCl is the correct formula for hydrochloric acid.
Zinc chloride is a common and well known salt.

2727.stem: Balancing Pb(NO3)2 -> PbO + NO2 + O2 is easiest if you treat the nitrate
2727.explanation: Nitrogen and oxygen must be counted individually here because the nitrate group is broken apart into different products.

options.text: as separate nitrogen and oxygen atoms

options.why: The group is destroyed in this reaction, so it cannot be carried across whole.
The nitrate is consumed, so it is not a catalyst.
A spectator is unchanged on both sides, which the nitrate clearly is not.

2727.stem: After balancing, a student finds a coefficient of one half. The correct next step is to
2727.explanation: Multiplying every coefficient by two clears the fraction and gives whole numbers throughout.

options.text: round the half up to one
options.why: Rounding destroys the balance that was just achieved.

options.text: leave the fraction as it is
options.why: Convention requires whole-number coefficients in a final equation.
This would introduce more fractions rather than removing them.

2727.stem: Which skeletal equation cannot be balanced, showing that one formula must be wrong?
2727.explanation: H2 + O2 -> H3O cannot balance with whole numbers because H3O is not a real neutral substance, so the formula is at fault.

options.why: This balances readily to 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O.
This is already balanced as written.
This balances readily to N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3.

2727.stem: Balance N2 + H2 -> NH3. The coefficient of H2 is
2727.explanation: One nitrogen molecule and three hydrogen molecules give two ammonia molecules, balancing six hydrogen atoms.

options.why: Two hydrogen molecules give four atoms, but six are needed for two ammonia molecules.
One hydrogen molecule gives only two atoms, far too few.
Six molecules give twelve atoms, which is twice too many.

2727.stem: The reason skeletal equations are taught before balanced ones is that
2727.explanation: Separating the task into identifying substances first and counting atoms second makes each step manageable and errors easier to find.

options.text: separating the two steps makes errors easier to find

options.why: A skeletal equation violates conservation of mass, so it is the less accurate form.
Balanced equations are used constantly for every calculation.
Formulae are essential to a skeletal equation.

2727.stem: A student cannot balance a skeletal equation after many attempts. The most likely cause, before assuming the reaction is impossible, is that
2727.explanation: A skeletal equation with correct formulae can always be balanced, so persistent failure points to a wrong formula rather than to impossible chemistry.

options.text: one of the formulae is wrong

options.why: Every real reaction conserves atoms and so can always be balanced.
Reversing the arrow does not change the atom counts on either side.
Omitting coefficients is what leaves an equation unbalanced in the first place.

2727.stem: Why does balancing never change the chemistry a skeletal equation describes?
2727.explanation: Coefficients only state how many units of each substance take part; the substances themselves are fixed by their formulae.

options.text: Balancing changes only the physical states
options.why: States are added separately and are unaffected by balancing.
The arrow is untouched throughout the process.
Spectators are removed when writing an ionic equation, which is a different step.

2727.stem: Two students balance the same skeletal equation and reach different but both-balanced answers. The most likely explanation is that
2727.explanation: One student has a multiple of the other's coefficients, since any balanced set stays balanced when every term is multiplied by the same number.

options.text: one set is a multiple of the other
one of them must be wrong
options.why: Both can be balanced; only one is in the smallest whole-number form.

options.text: the equation has two different reactions
options.why: The skeletal equation fixes a single reaction.
The rules are strict; only the overall scale is free.

2727.stem: In balancing a combustion equation, leaving free oxygen until last works because
2727.explanation: Oxygen appears in several products, so fixing those first determines how much oxygen is needed, and the free element can then absorb the total without disturbing anything.

options.text: its coefficient can absorb the total

options.why: Oxygen must balance like every other element.
Excess oxygen is an experimental condition, not a rule of balancing.

options.text: free elements have no atoms to count
options.why: Free elements have atoms and are counted in exactly the same way.

2727.stem: A skeletal equation contains a polyatomic group that survives unchanged on both sides. Treating that group as a unit is justified because
2727.explanation: If the group is never broken apart, counting it once is arithmetically identical to counting its atoms individually, and it is far less error-prone.

options.text: counting it whole gives the same result with fewer steps

options.why: They do need balancing; the shortcut is only about how they are counted.
It is genuinely transferred between substances, so it is not a catalyst.

options.text: groups have no atoms of their own
options.why: A polyatomic group is made entirely of atoms.

2727.stem: Which criticism of the statement 'a skeletal equation is simply a wrong equation' is strongest?
2727.explanation: A skeletal equation is correct about identity and direction, and incomplete only in quantity, so calling it simply wrong misrepresents what it does say.

options.text: It is in fact always balanced
options.why: By definition it is not yet balanced.
It identifies every substance and the direction of change.

options.text: It is only used by beginners
options.why: Experienced chemists write skeletal equations as a first step routinely.

2727.stem: A balanced equation is multiplied throughout by three. In terms of what the equation asserts about the world, this
2727.explanation: Multiplying every coefficient preserves all the ratios, so the chemical claim is identical and only the scale of description changes.

options.text: asserts exactly the same thing at a larger scale
asserts that three times as much reacts
options.why: The equation gives ratios, not absolute quantities, so no such claim is made.
Uniform multiplication preserves balance perfectly.
The formulae are untouched by multiplication.

2727.stem: Why can a skeletal equation be a useful record even before it is balanced?
2727.explanation: It already captures what reacts and what forms, which is the qualitative result of an experiment and is often what the chemist wants to record first.

options.text: It records the qualitative result of the experiment
It gives the yield of the reaction
options.why: Yield requires balanced coefficients and measured masses.
An unbalanced equation appears to contradict conservation of mass.
Mechanism concerns the steps between reactants and products and is not shown.

2727.stem: Balancing a skeletal equation by changing a subscript produces an equation with equal atom counts. The deepest objection is that
2727.explanation: The atom counts now balance for substances that are not the ones in the reaction, so the equation is internally consistent while describing something that never happened.

options.text: it balances a reaction that did not occur
the atom counts are still unequal
options.why: The objection stands even when the counts do come out equal.

options.text: subscripts are hard to write neatly
options.why: Presentation has nothing to do with the chemical error.

options.text: coefficients would be simpler to use
options.why: True but far too weak; the real point is that the chemistry has been changed.

2727.stem: Given a skeletal equation in which one element appears in three different compounds on the product side, the best balancing strategy is to
2727.explanation: Elements confined to one compound on each side should be fixed first, because each choice then constrains the rest and the scattered element is settled last.

options.text: fix the elements confined to one compound first

options.why: Every later adjustment would disturb it, forcing repeated rework.

options.text: balance the elements in alphabetical order
options.why: Alphabetical order bears no relation to how the constraints interact.
Guessing works eventually but is far slower than using the constraints.

2727.stem: A textbook writes a skeletal equation with a question mark where a product should be. This is best described as
2727.explanation: It is a partial skeletal equation used as a prompt, since the products are not yet stated and nothing can be balanced until they are.

options.text: a prompt, not an equation yet

options.why: A skeletal equation must name every substance on both sides.
Nothing can be balanced while a product is unknown.
The rest of it is written in formulae, not names.

2727.stem: Two skeletal equations describe the same reaction, but one includes water as a reactant and the other does not. Deciding which is right requires
2727.explanation: Experimental evidence about whether water is consumed decides the matter; both versions can be balanced, so balancing cannot settle it.

options.text: evidence about whether water is consumed
checking which one balances more easily
options.why: Ease of balancing says nothing about which chemistry is real.
The number of substances is a consequence of the chemistry, not a test of it.

options.text: seeing which is shorter to write
options.why: Brevity is not a criterion of chemical truth.

2727.stem: Why is it sound practice to check a balanced equation by recounting every element rather than only the ones just adjusted?
2727.explanation: Adjusting a coefficient changes every element in that formula at once, so an element settled earlier can easily have been knocked out of balance.

options.text: one adjustment changes every element in that formula
elements can change identity during balancing
options.why: Elements never change identity in a chemical reaction.
It is good practice for a concrete reason, not merely a convention.

options.text: only the last element ever matters
options.why: Every element must balance for the equation to be correct.

2728.stem: The law of conservation of mass states that in a chemical reaction, mass can be
2728.explanation: Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction; the atoms are only rearranged.

options.why: Creating mass would mean atoms appearing from nowhere.
Destroying mass would mean atoms vanishing entirely.
Neither happens in any chemical reaction.

2728.stem: The law of conservation of mass was established by
2728.explanation: Antoine Lavoisier established the law through careful weighing of reactions carried out in closed vessels.

options.why: Dalton proposed the atomic theory, which explained the law rather than establishing it.
Boyle is remembered for the gas law relating pressure and volume.
Mendeleev is remembered for the periodic table of the elements.

2728.stem: A chemical equation must be balanced in order to satisfy the law of
2728.explanation: Balancing makes the number of atoms of each element the same on both sides, which is conservation of mass expressed in symbols.

options.why: That law concerns the fixed composition of a compound, a related but different idea.
That law concerns two elements forming several compounds.
Momentum is a concept from physics and is unrelated to balancing equations.

2728.stem: In a reaction, 10 g of A reacts with 20 g of B in a sealed tube. The total mass of the products is
2728.explanation: In a sealed vessel nothing escapes, so the product mass equals the combined reactant mass of 30 g.

options.why: Uses only the mass of B and ignores A.
Uses only the mass of A and ignores B.
Multiplies the masses instead of adding them.

2728.stem: Conservation of mass holds in a chemical reaction because atoms are only
2728.explanation: A chemical reaction rearranges existing atoms into new combinations; no atom is made or lost.

options.why: Atoms are never created in a chemical reaction.
Atoms are never destroyed in a chemical reaction.
Changing one element into another requires a nuclear reaction.

2728.stem: A candle burning in an open dish appears to lose mass because
2728.explanation: Carbon dioxide and water vapour escape into the room and are never weighed, though their mass still exists.

options.text: gaseous products escape into the air
mass is destroyed by the flame
options.why: A flame cannot destroy matter, only rearrange it.
Wax is easily weighed, which is how the loss is noticed.
Heat is energy and carries no appreciable mass in a chemical reaction.

2728.stem: To demonstrate conservation of mass in the laboratory, the reaction must be carried out
2728.explanation: A closed or sealed vessel prevents any gas escaping, so nothing leaves the balance.

options.why: Any gas produced would escape and the mass would appear to fall.
Temperature does not affect whether mass is conserved.

options.text: over a long period of time
options.why: Duration has no bearing on the conservation of mass.

2728.stem: If 5 g of a compound decomposes into 3 g of solid and a gas, the mass of the gas is
2728.explanation: The mass of the gas must be the difference between the starting 5 g and the 3 g of solid left behind.

options.why: Adds the two masses instead of subtracting them.
Repeats the mass of the solid rather than finding the remainder.
Uses the whole starting mass and leaves nothing for the solid.

2728.stem: Which observation would appear to contradict the law of conservation of mass?
2728.explanation: Rusting in an open dish takes oxygen from the air, so the sample gains mass and the law seems to fail until the oxygen is accounted for.

options.text: An iron nail gaining mass as it rusts in air
Two solutions mixing with no change in mass
options.why: No change in mass is exactly what the law predicts.

options.text: A sealed flask showing constant mass
options.why: Constant mass in a sealed flask confirms the law.

options.text: A solid dissolving with no change in mass
options.why: Dissolving conserves mass and agrees with the law.

2728.stem: The law of conservation of mass applies to
2728.explanation: Both physical and chemical changes conserve mass, because in neither is matter created or destroyed.

options.why: Melting and dissolving conserve mass just as reactions do.
Chemical reactions conserve mass as strictly as physical changes.
The law is one of the most thoroughly tested in all of science.

2728.stem: In a balanced equation, the total number of atoms of each element on the left equals that on the right. This directly reflects
2728.explanation: Equal atom counts on both sides are the symbolic expression of mass being conserved.

options.why: Rate is not conveyed by a chemical equation.
Energy is shown separately, if at all, and not by the atom counts.
States are shown by symbols such as (s) and (g).

2728.stem: A student burns magnesium in an open crucible and finds the residue weighs more than the ribbon. The extra mass comes from
2728.explanation: Oxygen from the air combines with the magnesium, so the product contains atoms that were not on the balance to begin with.

options.why: Heat is energy and adds no measurable mass.
The crucible is weighed along with its contents both times.
The gain is real and is reproduced every time the experiment is done.

2728.stem: Conservation of mass is best tested using a reaction that
2728.explanation: A reaction producing no gas keeps everything in the vessel, so mass can be compared without needing a seal.

options.text: produces a great deal of gas
options.why: Escaping gas makes the test harder unless the vessel is sealed.
Duration only increases the chance of accidental loss.
Strong heating tends to drive off volatile products.

2728.stem: Which of these would NOT be explained by the law of conservation of mass?
2728.explanation: How fast a reaction proceeds is a matter of kinetics, about which conservation of mass says nothing at all.

options.text: why one reaction is faster than another

options.why: Balancing exists precisely to satisfy this law.

options.text: why a sealed flask keeps constant mass
options.why: Constant mass in a sealed flask is a direct consequence of the law.
The gain is the mass of oxygen added, fully accounted for by the law.

2728.stem: In an experiment, 4.8 g of magnesium burns completely to give 8.0 g of magnesium oxide. The mass of oxygen used is
2728.explanation: Conservation of mass requires the oxygen to make up the difference between 8.0 g and 4.8 g.

options.why: Adds the two masses rather than subtracting them.
Repeats the mass of magnesium rather than finding the difference.
Uses the whole product mass and leaves nothing for the magnesium.

2728.stem: Sodium sulphate solution and barium chloride solution are mixed in a sealed flask on a balance. The reading
2728.explanation: A precipitate forms but nothing enters or leaves the flask, so the total mass is unchanged.

options.why: The precipitate is still inside the flask and still on the balance.
No matter enters the flask, so the mass cannot rise.
There is no mechanism for the mass to change in either direction.

2728.stem: 12 g of carbon burns in 32 g of oxygen. If 40 g of carbon dioxide is collected, the most likely explanation is
2728.explanation: The expected product mass is 44 g, so 4 g has been lost during collection rather than destroyed.

options.text: 4 g of product escaped during collection

options.why: Mass is never destroyed in a chemical reaction.
Unreacted carbon would leave a solid residue, not reduce the gas collected.

options.text: the law does not apply to gases
options.why: The law applies to gases exactly as it does to solids and liquids.

2728.stem: Which experimental design best demonstrates conservation of mass to a class?
2728.explanation: A sealed flask on a balance lets the class watch a visible reaction occur while the reading stays fixed.

options.text: A sealed flask on a balance during a visible reaction
An open beaker with an effervescing mixture
options.why: The escaping gas makes the mass fall, which looks like the law failing.

options.text: A crucible heated over a flame in air
options.why: Oxygen from the air can join the sample and change the reading.

options.text: A solution left to evaporate overnight
options.why: The solvent escapes and the mass falls sharply.

2728.stem: A student proposes that burning is the one exception to conservation of mass. The best refutation is to
2728.explanation: Burning a sample inside a sealed container shows the mass staying constant, because the gaseous products cannot escape.

options.text: burn a sample inside a sealed container
burn a larger sample in the open
options.why: A larger open sample simply loses more gas and reinforces the misconception.
Weighing the ash alone is exactly the mistake that creates the misconception.
Repetition of a flawed method just reproduces the same apparent loss.

2728.stem: In the reaction 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, if 4 g of hydrogen reacts with 32 g of oxygen, the mass of water formed is
2728.explanation: All the reactants are used up, so the water formed weighs the sum of the two reactant masses.

options.why: Uses only the mass of oxygen and ignores the hydrogen.
Subtracts the masses instead of adding them.
Uses only the mass of hydrogen and ignores the oxygen.

2728.stem: Why does the law of conservation of mass make it impossible for an element to appear on only one side of a balanced equation?
2728.explanation: Atoms cannot be created or destroyed, so any atom present among the reactants must appear somewhere among the products and vice versa.

options.text: Its atoms would have to appear from nowhere or vanish

options.why: Appearance is not the issue; the atom counts are.

options.text: Every element must be in every compound
options.why: No such requirement exists in chemistry.
Free elements change sides constantly in displacement reactions.

2728.stem: A sealed flask containing a reaction is weighed, opened, and weighed again, showing a lower mass. This shows that
2728.explanation: Gas that had been trapped escaped when the flask was opened, so the loss is a transfer of matter out of the system.

options.text: gas escaped when the seal was broken

options.why: Opening a container cannot destroy anything.

options.text: the law failed inside the flask
options.why: The law held perfectly while the flask was sealed, as the first weighing showed.
The drop is exactly what escaping gas predicts, so no misreading is needed.

2728.stem: Two students heat the same mass of a metal in air. One works in an open dish, the other in a sealed tube. Comparing final masses, the open dish will show
2728.explanation: The open dish can take in oxygen from the surrounding air, so the sample gains mass, while the sealed tube has only the oxygen already inside.

options.text: a larger gain, because more oxygen is available
a larger loss, because gas escapes
options.why: The metal takes in oxygen rather than giving off a gas.
Oxidation of a metal in air changes the mass measurably.
The supply of oxygen differs between the two set-ups.

2728.stem: In which case can the mass of a system legitimately increase during a chemical change?
2728.explanation: If the system is open, matter can enter it from outside, so a substance combining with oxygen from the air gains mass.

options.text: When an open vessel takes in a gas
When the system is sealed and airtight
options.why: Nothing can enter a sealed system, so its mass is fixed.

options.text: When a great deal of heat is supplied
options.why: Heat adds no measurable mass in a chemical change.
Rusting in open air increases the mass of the iron sample.

2728.stem: 16 g of methane burns completely. If 44 g of carbon dioxide and 36 g of water are produced, the mass of oxygen consumed is
2728.explanation: The total product mass of 80 g must equal the methane plus the oxygen, so the oxygen accounts for 80 minus 16.

options.why: Uses the total product mass without subtracting the methane.
Subtracts the two product masses from each other.
Repeats the mass of the methane rather than finding the oxygen.

2728.stem: Why is the law of conservation of mass better tested with a precipitation reaction than with an effervescence?
2728.explanation: A precipitate stays in the vessel and remains on the balance, whereas effervescence releases a gas that escapes unless the vessel is sealed.

options.text: The precipitate stays in the vessel

options.why: Speed is irrelevant to whether mass can be measured accurately.
Absolute weight is not the issue; staying in the vessel is.

options.text: Effervescence is not a chemical change
options.why: Effervescence from a reaction is certainly a chemical change.

2728.stem: A reaction in a sealed flask shows a constant mass but a rising temperature. This shows that
2728.explanation: Mass is conserved while energy is released, which means mass and energy changes are independent in ordinary chemistry.

options.text: mass is conserved even when energy is released

options.why: Any mass change from energy release is far too small to measure chemically.
The rising temperature shows a reaction is definitely occurring.
A leak would change the mass, which is observed to be constant.

2728.stem: Why did chemists before Lavoisier believe that burning destroyed matter?
2728.explanation: They weighed only what remained in the open vessel and did not capture the gaseous products, so burning appeared to lose mass.

options.text: They did not capture the gaseous products
Their balances were too crude to use
options.why: Balances of adequate sensitivity existed; the method was the problem.
The laws of nature do not change with the century.

options.text: They never weighed anything at all
options.why: They weighed carefully, but only the solid residue.

2728.stem: A student claims conservation of mass fails in nuclear reactions. The most accurate response is
2728.explanation: In nuclear reactions a measurable amount of mass is converted into energy, so mass alone is not conserved, though mass and energy together are. Chemical reactions are unaffected.

options.text: correct for nuclear reactions, but not for chemical ones
wrong, because mass is always conserved
options.why: Nuclear reactions genuinely convert a measurable mass into energy.

options.text: correct, so chemical equations need not balance
options.why: Chemical reactions involve no measurable mass change, so balancing still holds.
